In Joseph Priestley's time, scientists were not aware about the energy,
but later on by performing different experiments much was discovered
about it.
Energy is released when carbondioxide and water are formed by
combining oxygen molecules with carbon and hydrogen.

Scientists have come to know that energy released during oxygen

x Where did this energy come from?
A Dutch scientist, Jan Ingenhousz (1730-1799), found the answer.
To
know about how the plants release oxygen he studied continuously.
In 1779,
he noticed that plants form oxygen only in the presence of light.
In an experiment with the aquatic plant, Hydrilla (submerged, rootless
water plant), he observed that in bright sunlight, small bubbles were formed
around the green parts while in the dark they did not form.
He also found
that the gas present in the bubbles was oxygen.
It was further confirmed when Engelman in the early 20 th century
ingeniously detected the point of maximum rate of photosynthesis.
He
used a group of algae and exposed it to different colours of light the colours
that we see in a rainbow.
Then he used oxygen sensitive bacteria and found
that they crowd around areas illuminated with bright red and blue rays of
light.
This led to the studies on effect of light on photosynthesis, the role
of different coloured compounds called pigments in plants and the
utilization of light energy.

parsed_output.answer: To study the presence of starch in leaves, the following process is followed in the laboratory: First, a thin leaf is taken from a plant exposed to sunlight. The leaf is boiled in water to kill the cells and then transferred to methylated spirit to remove chlorophyll, making the leaf pale. After that, the leaf is spread on a petridish and a few drops of iodine solution are added. If starch is present, the leaf turns bluish-black. This indicates the presence of starch, which is a product of photosynthesis.

required_point_details.point: Use a sun-exposed leaf and boil it in water
Remove chlorophyll using alcohol in a water bath
Add iodine solution
A blue-black colour shows starch

We eat various types of food which pass through the same digestive
tract.
It is to be converted to substances small enough to be utilised

1.5.1 Passage of food through alimentary canal or gut
Food is cut and crushed by our teeth in the
mouth and mixed with saliva to make it wet and
slippery lump called bolus (This process is called
as mastication).
This bolus is suitable to pass
through oesophagus.
Saliva is secreted by three pairs
of salivary glands.
Saliva mainly contains an enzyme
amylase (ptyalin) which help in the breakdown of
complex carbohydrates into simple ones.
This
process of breaking down larger complex substances
into simple ones with the help of enzymes is called digestion.
The
tongue helps in mixing the food and pushing it into the next part.
The
lower jaw also helps in this process.

The soft food mixed with saliva passes through oesophagus or food
pipe by wave like movements called peristaltic movement to the stomach.
In the stomach, food gets churned with gastric juice and HCl rendering the
medium acidic.
Now the food is in semisolid condition.
The digestion of
food goes on as most of the proteins are broken down into smaller
molecules with the help of enzyme pepsin.
Nutrition 16
Food in the form of a soft slimy substance where some proteins and
carbohydrates have already been broken down is called chyme.
Now the
food material passes from the stomach to the small intestine.
Here the
ring like muscles called pyloric sphincters relax to open the passage into
the small intestine.
The sphincters are responsible for regulating the
opening of the passage such that only small quantities of the food material
may be passed into the small intestine at a time.
The small intestine is the longest part of the
alimentary canal.
Its proximal part is called duodenum.
It is the site of further digestion of carbohydrates,
proteins and fats.
It receives the secretion of liver and
pancreas for this purpose.
These juices render the internal
condition of the intestine gradually to a basic or alkaline one.
Fats are digested by converting them into small globule
like forms by the help of the bile juice secreted from liver.
This process is called emulsification.
Pancreatic juice secreted from pancreas contains enzymes like trypsin
for carrying on the process of digestion of proteins and lipase for fats.
Walls of the small intestine secrete intestinal juice (Succusentericus)
which carry this process further that is small molecules of proteins are
broken down to further smaller molecules.
The same is the condition with
fats.
Carbohydrate digestion that started in the mouth and did not occur in
the stomach, resumes now as the medium gradually changes to an alkaline
one and the enzymes become active for complete carbohydrate breakdown.

curd that we eat is processed from milk, which comes from a cow, which

The grass carries out photosynthesis and prepares food.
In every case, the origin of food materials can be traced back to green
plants.
Once the food is eaten, its energy follows a variety of pattern through
the organisms.
Not all the food can be fully digested and assimilated.
Hair,
feathers, insect exoskeletons, cartilage and bone in animal foods, cellulose
and lignin in plant foods cannot be digested by the most animals.
These
materials are either ejected by defecation or regurgitated as indigested
remains.
Assimilated energy (that is not lost through respiration or excretion)
is available for the synthesis of new biomass through growth and
reproduction.
Organisms lose some biomass by death, disease or annual
leaf-drop, where they enter the detritus pathways of the food chain i.e.,
after the death and decomposition of organisms the materials flow back
into the environment(soil, water, air).
The remaining biomass is eventually
consumed by herbivores or predators and its energy there by enters the
next higher trophic level in the ecosystem.
The materials keep on cycling i.e. entering the living beings and through
death and decay returning to the soil and atmosphere Such a flow of
materials between organisms and their environment is called Cycling of
materials or mineral circulation or Biogeochemical cycles (You have
learnt in class IX ).
Energy enters the producers in the ecosystem from the sun in
the form of solar energy or solar radiation.

organisms use most of the food energy that they assimilate into their bodies

reproduction.
Because biological energy transformations are inefficient,
a substantial proportion of metabolized food energy is lost, unused as
heat.
Hence pyramid of energy is always upright.
Only a small fraction goes to the eater at next trophic level.
Organisms

Most of the
energy in petrol is lost as heat in a car’s engine rather than being
transformed into the energy of motion.
In natural communities, energy
used to perform work or dissipated as heat cannot be consumed by other
organism and is forever lost to the ecosystem.

parsed_output.answer: To understand anaerobic respiration in the school laboratory, you can follow a procedure that involves testing for the production of carbon dioxide and heat. First, you need to prepare a glucose solution and remove the dissolved oxygen from it by heating and cooling the solution without shaking. Then, add yeast to the solution. To prevent oxygen from entering, pour a layer of liquid paraffin on top of the mixture. This creates an anaerobic environment. Next, attach a tube to the mixture leading to a bicarbonate/indicator solution (like lime water) to detect the release of carbon dioxide, which will turn the lime water milky. Additionally, use a thermometer to observe any change in temperature, indicating the release of heat during the process. This experiment helps demonstrate how anaerobic respiration produces carbon dioxide and heat without the presence of oxygen.

3.3 Blood vessels and circulation
Let us study about the structure and functions of the blood vessels
along with their discovery.
It was not until 16th century that we really came to know how our blood
vessels function.
In 1574, an Italian doctor, Girolamo Fabrici, was studying
the veins in the leg.
He noticed that they had small valves in them that
permited blood to flow towards heart.
These were one-way valves that
checked backflow of blood.
Movement of leg muscle helps in movement
of blood through veins.
Everyone thought that the blood leaving the left ventricle always moved
away from the heart for which Fabrici paid no attention.
He missed the
importance of his own discovery.
Circulation58
William Harvey (1578-1657), an English doctor, went to Italy for
further education under Fabrici.
Harvey dissected the hearts of dead people and studied the valves
between each atrium and its ventricle.
He noticed that they were oneway valves.
They allowed the blood to flow from the atrium to the
ventricle without any hinderance.
However, when the heart contracts,
blood in the ventricle could not flow back into the atrium.
Instead, the
blood was pushed out into the arteries.
Harvey began thinking about the valves his teacher, Fabrici, had
discovered in the leg veins.
They were one-way, and they forced the blood
to move toward the heart.
He checked that by tying off and blocking different veins in animals.
He found that the veins always bulged on the side of the block away from
the heart.
As though the blood was trying to flow toward the heart.
This
was true of all veins.
In the arteries, the blood bulged on the heart side of any block he put
in, as though it were trying to flow away from the heart and couldn’t move
in the other direction.
Harvey now saw what was happening.
The heart pushed blood in to the
arteries and the blood returned by way of the veins.
It did this for both
ventricles.
The blood had a double circulation.
Starting from the right
ventricle blood left by way of the arteries to the lungs and returned by way
of veins to the left atrium, this is known as ‘pulmonary circulation’.
From there it flowed into the left ventricle and left by way of aorta to the
rest of the body and returned by way of the veins to the right atrium.
From
here it moved into the right ventricle, this is known as ‘systemic
circulation’.
As blood reaches the heart two times through pulmonary
cycle and again through systemic, it is called ‘double circulation’.

parsed_output.answer: Double circulation is a process in which blood passes through the heart twice during one complete cycle. In humans, this system is important because it ensures that oxygenated and deoxygenated blood are separated, allowing for efficient oxygen delivery to the body and removal of carbon dioxide. The process involves two separate circulations: pulmonary circulation and systemic circulation. Pulmonary circulation carries deoxygenated blood from the right ventricle to the lungs, where it gets oxygenated, and returns it to the left atrium. Systemic circulation then carries oxygenated blood from the left ventricle to the rest of the body, where it delivers oxygen and picks up carbon dioxide, before returning to the right atrium. This separation of blood ensures that the body receives a continuous supply of oxygen and nutrients while efficiently removing waste products.

parsed_output.answer: Arteries and veins are both types of blood vessels, but they have different structures and functions. Arteries carry blood away from the heart to the body parts, and they have thick, elastic walls that can withstand high pressure. Veins carry blood back to the heart from the body parts, and they have thinner walls. Arteries do not have valves, while veins have valves that prevent the backflow of blood. The blood in arteries is usually oxygenated, except for the pulmonary artery, which carries deoxygenated blood to the lungs. The blood in veins is usually deoxygenated, except for the pulmonary veins, which carry oxygenated blood from the lungs.

parsed_output.answer:
Excretion is the process by which living organisms remove waste products and excess substances from their bodies. These wastes are generated as a result of various metabolic activities, such as respiration, digestion, and other cellular processes. The waste products include substances like carbon dioxide, water, nitrogenous compounds (like ammonia, urea, and uric acid), excess salts, and other harmful materials. If these wastes are not removed, they can be toxic and harmful to the body. Excretion ensures that these wastes are eliminated from the body to maintain homeostasis.

The process of urine formation involves several steps. First, the kidneys filter the blood through tiny structures called nephrons. In the glomerulus of the nephron, blood is filtered, and useful substances like water, glucose, and ions are reabsorbed back into the bloodstream. Meanwhile, waste products and excess substances are secreted into the tubules. The remaining fluid, now called urine, is collected in the renal pelvis and transported through the ureters to the urinary bladder. The urine is then stored in the bladder until it is expelled from the body through the urethra during urination.

The rhesus factor
There is another antigen of red blood cells which is present in 85% of the people of
Britain, this is known as the Rhesus factor, as it was first discovered in Rhesus monkeys.
People who have this are said to be Rhesus positive (Rh+).
Those who do not have this
factor are termed Rhesus negative (Rh-).
Normally they do not carry an antibody to this
factor in their plasma.
However, if Rh+ blood is transfused into the blood of a Rh- person,
against Rh-factors will be formed and these are capable of destroying Rh+ red cells.
Under
certain circumstances this is a potential hazard for babies.
If a Rh+ man marries a Rh- woman, some of the children are likely to be Rh+.
At birth
there is always some mixing of blood between the circulation of mother and baby and this
may occasionally happen during pregnancy.
So, if a child is Rh+ some of its blood will leak
into its mother’s circulation and cause antibodies to form in her blood.
If the mother has
more children, not all will necessarily be Rh+, but if they are, the amount of antibodies in
her blood often increases with each pregnancy, and in some instances the antibodies in her
blood may pass into the baby’s blood in sufficient quantities to produce very serious anaemia
and even death.
Fortunately these cases are not frequent, and when they do occur, the baby
is given a complete transfusion soon after birth so that the baby’s blood is replaced by
blood containing no antibodies to the rhesus factor.
It is now possible for this transfusion
to be carrried out before birth.
Another recently developed technique is for the mother to
be given an injection shortly after the birth of her first child which prevents the Rh+ cells
from stimulating the production of the harmful antibody.

4.6 Dialysis Machine (Artificial kidney)
Kidneys are vital organs for survival.
Several factors like infections, injury, very
high blood pressure, very high blood sugar
or restricted blood flow to kidneys leads to
accumulation of poisonous wastes in the
body and leads to death.
Dialysis machine is used to filter the
blood of a person when both kidneys are
damaged.
The process is called
‘haemodialysis’.
In this process, blood is taken out from the main artery,
mixed with an anticoagulant, such as heparin, and then pumped into the
apparatus called dialyzer.
In this apparatus blood flows through channels
or tubes which are madeup of cellophane.
These tubes are embedded in
the dialyzing fluid.
A thin membrane separates the blood flowing inside
the tube and dialyzing fluid (dialysis), which has the same composition as
that of plasma, except the nitrogenous wastes.
As nitrogenous wastes are absent in dialyzing fluids, these substances
from the blood move out freely, there by cleaning the blood of its wastes.
This process is called "dialysis".
This is similar to the function of the
kidney, but is different as there is no reabsorption involved .The cleaned
blood is pumped back to the body through a vein after adding anti-coagulant
(heparin).
Each dialysis session lasts for 3 to 6 hours.
This method has
been using for thousands of uremic / kidney failure patients all over the
world.

parsed_output.answer: Some people need to use a dialysis machine because their kidneys are damaged and cannot properly filter waste products from their blood. The kidneys play a vital role in removing toxins, excess water, and other harmful substances from the body. When the kidneys fail to function, these wastes accumulate in the blood, leading to serious health issues and even death. Dialysis is a medical treatment that mimics the function of healthy kidneys by filtering the blood. The principle involved in dialysis is called 'haemodialysis'. In this process, blood is taken from the patient's artery, mixed with an anticoagulant to prevent clotting, and then passed through a dialyzer. The dialyzer contains a thin membrane that separates the blood from a dialyzing fluid. This fluid has a composition similar to plasma but lacks nitrogenous wastes. As a result, waste substances from the blood move into the dialyzing fluid, cleaning the blood. The cleaned blood is then returned to the patient's body through a vein. This process helps remove toxins and maintain the balance of water and electrolytes in the body.

parsed_output.answer: Phototropism in plants occurs when the plant bends towards a light source. This response is due to the plant's ability to sense light and the distribution of a chemical called auxin. When light hits one side of the plant, more auxin accumulates on the shaded side. Auxin causes the cells on the shaded side to grow faster, making the plant bend towards the light. This was demonstrated by Charles Darwin and his son Francis Darwin, who found that the tip of the plant (coleoptile) is responsible for sensing light. Further experiments by F.W. Went showed that the bending is caused by a chemical stimulus, which is now known as auxin. The auxin is produced in the tip of the plant and moves down to the stem, causing the cells on the shaded side to elongate more, leading to the bending of the stem towards the light.

2.8 Evolution in gases exchanging system
Exchange of gases is a common life process in all living organisms,
but it is not same in all.
Single celled organisms Amoeba or multicellular
organisms like Hydra, Planaria, roundworms and earthworms obtain
oxygen and expel carbon dioxide directly from the body by the process of
diffusion.
In other multicellular animals special organs are evolved.
Animals
either terrestrial or aquatic adapted to different types of respiration and
possess different types of respiratory organs mostly depending on the
habitat in which they live.
Body size, availability of water and the type of
their circulatory system are some of the factors for the animals to develop
different types of respiratory organs.
There is tracheal respiratory system in insects like cockroach,
grasshopper etc.
Tracheal respiratory system consists of series of tubes
called trachea.
This is divided into fine branches called tracheoles which
carry air directly to the cells in the tissues.
Some aquatic animals like fishes have developed special organs for
respiration which are known as gills or branchiae.
Blood supplied to gills
through capillaries which have thin walls where gases are exchanged.
This
is called branchial respiration (gill respiration).
Fish keeps its mouth open
and lowers the floor of the oral cavity.
As a result water from outside will
be drawn into the oral cavity.
Now the mouth is closed and the floor of the
oral cavity is raised.
Water is pushed into the pharynx and is forced to gill
pouches through internal branchial apertures.
Gill lamellae are bathed with
water and absorbs the oxygen dissolved in the water.

2.9.1 Transportation of gases in plants
The stomatal openings lead to a series of spaces
between the cells inside the plant.
Which form a
continuous network all over the plant.
The spaces
are very large in the leaves, much smaller in other
parts of the plant.
The air spaces are lined with water
where the oxygen is dissolved in this and passes
through the porous cell walls into the cytoplasm.
Here the glucose is broken down into carbon dioxide
and water with the liberation of the energy.
The
energy released is stored in mitochondria in the form
of A TP to perform metabolic activities.
The carbon dioxide passes out into the air spaces
by a similar method.
The whole system works by
diffusion as the oxygen is used up by the cells a
gradient develops between the cells and the air in
the spaces.

parsed_output.answer: Mitosis and meiosis are two types of cell division, but they have several key differences. Mitosis occurs in all body cells and results in two daughter cells that are genetically identical to the parent cell. It retains the same number of chromosomes (2n). Meiosis, on the other hand, occurs only in sex cells (gametes) and results in four daughter cells that have half the number of chromosomes (n). This is called reduction division. Mitosis is a single process, while meiosis consists of two phases. Additionally, meiosis involves the pairing and exchange of genetic material between homologous chromosomes, which does not occur in mitosis. These differences are important for understanding how organisms grow, repair, and reproduce.

parsed_output.answer: The acid-and-leaf experiment is used to model how the stomach is protected from its own acid. In this experiment, two similar green leaves are taken. One leaf is coated with petroleum jelly or grease, while the other is left untreated. A weak acid is then applied to both leaves. After some time, the leaf without the grease or petroleum jelly is affected by the acid, while the leaf coated with grease remains unaffected. This is because the grease acts like the mucus lining in the stomach, which protects the stomach walls from the strong acid. The mucus lining in the stomach forms a thin protective layer that counteracts the action of the acid, similar to how petroleum jelly protects the leaf. This experiment demonstrates that the mucus lining in the stomach is crucial for protecting it from its own digestive juices.

parsed_output.answer: Mendel’s monohybrid experiment involved studying the inheritance of a single trait, such as seed color in pea plants. He selected two purebred pea plants—one with yellow seeds and one with green seeds. When he crossed these plants, all the offspring in the first generation (F1) had yellow seeds. This demonstrated that the yellow seed color was dominant over the green seed color. When these F1 plants were allowed to self-pollinate, the second generation (F2) showed a 3:1 ratio of yellow to green seeds. This ratio indicated that the recessive trait (green seeds) reappeared in the F2 generation. This experiment demonstrated Mendel’s Law of Dominance, which states that in a pair of alleles, the dominant trait is expressed in the presence of the recessive trait.

parsed_output.answer: In humans, sex determination occurs through the combination of sex chromosomes inherited from the parents. The father contributes either an X or a Y chromosome, while the mother always contributes an X chromosome. If the father's sperm carries an X chromosome, the resulting zygote will have XX chromosomes and develop into a female. If the sperm carries a Y chromosome, the zygote will have XY chromosomes and develop into a male. This process is explained in the textbook, which states that females have two X chromosomes (XX) and males have one X and one Y chromosome (XY). The gametes from the father are of two types: one with an X chromosome and one with a Y chromosome. The mother's gametes (ova) always have an X chromosome. The sex of the baby is determined at the moment of fertilization when the sperm and egg combine.

parsed_output.answer: The use of toxic materials, such as pesticides, can have harmful effects on an ecosystem. These materials can enter the food chain through various ways, such as being absorbed by plants or water, and then consumed by animals. This process is known as bioaccumulation, where toxic substances accumulate in the bodies of organisms over time. As these toxins move up the food chain, their concentration increases at each level, a process called biomagnification. This means that top-level consumers, such as large fish or birds of prey, end up with the highest concentrations of toxins, which can lead to serious health problems or even death. The use of toxic materials can disrupt the balance of an ecosystem, harm wildlife, and affect human health as well.

parsed_output.answer: Recharging groundwater sources is important because it helps maintain a steady supply of water for future use. Groundwater is a crucial source of freshwater, and if it is not recharged, it can get depleted quickly. The textbook mentions that in the case of Kothapally village, farmers recharged their groundwater resources by building dykes or barriers in nearby canals and retaining rainwater. This helped restore and conserve groundwater, ensuring it is not depleted. Additionally, the textbook highlights that if we do not take care of water sources, there may not be enough water for future needs, and we might have to depend on other states or countries for water. Therefore, recharging groundwater is essential for sustainable water management and to prevent scarcity.

parsed_output.answer: We prefer a convex mirror as a rear-view mirror in vehicles because it provides a wider field of view compared to a concave mirror. When parallel rays of light fall on a convex mirror, they appear to diverge after reflection. By extending these reflected rays backwards, they seem to meet at a point called the focus. This property of convex mirrors allows them to form virtual, erect, and diminished images of objects behind the mirror. As a result, convex mirrors help drivers see a larger area behind the vehicle, which enhances safety.

parsed_output.answer: To find the distance of the image formed by a concave mirror, we use the mirror formula: 1/f = 1/v + 1/u. Here, the object is placed at a distance of 10 cm in front of the mirror, so u = -10 cm (negative because the object is on the same side as the incoming light). The radius of curvature (R) is given as 8 cm, so the focal length (f) is half of the radius of curvature, which is f = R/2 = 8/2 = 4 cm. Since it is a concave mirror, the focal length is negative, so f = -4 cm. Substituting these values into the mirror formula: 1/(-4) = 1/v + 1/(-10). Solving this equation gives 1/v = 1/(-4) - 1/(-10) = -1/4 + 1/10 = -5/20 + 2/20 = -3/20. Therefore, v = -20/3 ≈ -6.67 cm. The negative sign indicates that the image is formed on the same side as the object, which is the real image.

2.1.2 Balancing Chemical Equations
According to the law of conservation of mass, the total mass of the
products formed in chemical reaction must be equal to the total mass of
reactants consumed.
You know that an atom is the smallest particle of an
element that takes part in a chemical reaction.
It is the atom which accounts
for the mass of any substance.
As per the law of conservatioin of mass the
number of atoms of each element before and after reaction must be the
same.
26 Chemical Equations
All the chemical equations must be balanced, because atoms are neither
created nor destroyed in chemical reactions.
A chemical equation in which
the number of atoms of different elements on the reactant side (left side)
are same as those on product side (right side) is called a balanced reaction.
Formula units:
Balancing a chemical equation involves finding out how many
formula units of each substance take part in the reaction.as the name
implies, is one unit – whether atom, ion or molecule – corresponding to a
given formula.
One formula unit of NaCl for example is one Na+ (Sodium
ion) and one Cl– (Chlorine ion); one formula unit of MgBr2 is one Mg2+
ion and two Br– ions and one formula unit of water is one H2O molecule.
Now let us balance the chemical equation using a systematic method.
For this take the example of hydrogen reacting with oxygen to form water.

parsed_output.answer: A balanced chemical equation provides several important pieces of information. First, it shows the reactants and products involved in a chemical reaction through their chemical symbols and formulae. Second, it indicates the ratio of molecules of reactants and products, which helps in understanding the stoichiometry of the reaction. Third, it gives the relative masses of the reactants and products, which can be used to calculate the mass relationships in the reaction. Additionally, it can provide information about the physical states of the substances, heat changes (whether the reaction is exothermic or endothermic), gases evolved, and precipitates formed. Finally, it allows for the calculation of volumes, number of molecules, and other quantitative relationships based on the molar mass and Avogadro's number.

According to the law of conservation of mass, the total mass of the
products formed in chemical reaction must be equal to the total mass of
reactants consumed.
You know that an atom is the smallest particle of an
element that takes part in a chemical reaction.
It is the atom which accounts
for the mass of any substance.

number of atoms of each element before and after reaction must be the
same.

All the chemical equations must be balanced, because atoms are neither
created nor destroyed in chemical reactions.
A chemical equation in which
the number of atoms of different elements on the reactant side (left side)
are same as those on product side (right side) is called a balanced reaction.

formula units of each substance take part in the reaction.as the name
implies, is one unit – whether atom, ion or molecule – corresponding to a
given formula.

ion) and one Cl– (Chlorine ion); one formula unit of MgBr2 is one Mg2+
ion and two Br– ions and one formula unit of water is one H2O molecule.

3.6.2 Importance of pH in everyday life
1.
Are plants and animals pH sensitive?
Living organisms can survive only in a narrow range of pH change.

When acid
rain flows in to the rivers, it lowers the pH of the river water, the survival
of aquatic life in such rivers becomes difficult.
2.
Is pH change cause of tooth decay?
Tooth decay starts when the pH of the mouth is lower than 5.5.
Tooth enamel, made of calcium phosphate is the hardest substance
in the body.
It does not dissolve in water, but is corroded when the
pH in the mouth is below 5.5.
Bacteria present in the mouth produce
acids by degradation of sugar and food particles remaining in the
mouth.
The best way to prevent this is to clean the mouth after
eating food.
Using tooth pastes, which are generally basic neutralize
the excess acid and prevent tooth decay.

acid.

To get rid of this pain, people use bases called antacids.
These
antacids neutralize the excess acid in the stomach.
Magnesium hydroxide
(milk of magnesia), a mild base, is often used for this purpose.

parsed_output.answer: Tooth decay starts when the pH of the mouth is lower than 5.5 because the enamel of the teeth, which is made of calcium phosphate, begins to dissolve in acidic conditions. The pH scale measures the concentration of hydrogen ions (H3O+) in a solution. When the pH is below 5.5, the concentration of H3O+ ions is high enough to corrode the enamel. This happens because bacteria in the mouth break down sugars and food particles, producing acids. These acids lower the pH in the mouth, leading to tooth decay. Maintaining a pH above 5.5 helps prevent this corrosion and protects the teeth.

parsed_output.answer: The lens maker’s formula is given by: (n - 1) (1/R1 - 1/R2) = 1/f, where n is the refractive index of the lens material, R1 and R2 are the radii of curvature of the two surfaces of the lens, and f is the focal length of the lens. This formula is derived based on the refraction of light through the curved surfaces of the lens. The term (n - 1) represents the difference between the refractive index of the lens and the surrounding medium (usually air). The terms 1/R1 and 1/R2 are related to the curvature of the lens surfaces, with R1 being the radius of curvature of the first surface and R2 being the radius of curvature of the second surface. The focal length f is the distance from the lens to the point where parallel rays converge (for a converging lens) or appear to diverge from (for a diverging lens).

parsed_output.answer: An orbital is a region in an atom where there is a high probability of finding an electron. It is a concept from the quantum mechanical model of the atom, which describes the probability distribution of an electron around the nucleus. In contrast, Bohr’s orbit refers to the fixed circular paths that electrons are thought to follow around the nucleus in his model. Bohr’s model suggested that electrons revolve in specific, quantized orbits at fixed distances from the nucleus, and they emit or absorb energy when transitioning between these orbits. However, the quantum mechanical model, developed by Schrödinger, replaced the idea of fixed orbits with orbitals, which are not defined paths but regions of space where electrons are likely to be found. This model better explains the behavior of electrons and accounts for phenomena like the splitting of spectral lines that Bohr’s model could not.

parsed_output.answer: Mendeleev’s periodic table had several limitations. One major limitation was the presence of anomalous pairs of elements, where elements with higher atomic weights were placed before those with lower atomic weights, such as tellurium (Te) and iodine (I). Additionally, dissimilar elements were sometimes placed in the same group, like cobalt (Co) and nickel (Ni), which have different properties. Mendeleev’s table also did not leave room for new elements, and it was based on atomic weight rather than atomic number, which led to inaccuracies in predicting properties. The modern periodic table addresses these limitations by arranging elements based on their atomic number, which provides a more accurate and consistent basis for predicting properties. It also correctly places elements in groups based on their electronic configurations, ensuring that elements with similar properties are grouped together. Furthermore, the modern table accounts for all known elements and allows for the prediction of new elements with greater accuracy.

parsed_output.answer: Ohm’s law states that the potential difference (V) across a conductor is directly proportional to the current (I) passing through it, provided the temperature remains constant. Mathematically, this is expressed as V = IR, where R is the resistance of the conductor. To verify Ohm’s law, an experiment can be conducted using a circuit with a battery, ammeter, voltmeter, and a conductor (like an iron spoke). The procedure involves connecting the conductor to the battery and measuring the current and potential difference for different numbers of cells (from 1 to 5). For each case, the ratio V/I is calculated. If the ratio remains constant, it confirms Ohm’s law. A graph of V vs. I should be a straight line passing through the origin. This experiment also shows that materials like LEDs do not obey Ohm’s law, as their V/I ratio is not constant, resulting in a curved graph.

A closed path created by the connecting

flow is called a circuit.
For a continuous flow of

between.
Usually a gap is provided in the circuit by an electric switch that
can be opened or closed to either cut off or allow current flow through the
circuit.
Circuits may have more than one device (called as component)
that receives electric energy from the source.
These devices are commonly
connected in the circuit either in series or in parallel.
When the components of the circuit are connected in series, there
will be a single path for flow of electrons between the terminals of the
battery, generator or wall socket (which is simply and extension of these
terminals).
When these components are connected in parallel, they form
branches and each branch provides a separate path for the flow of electrons.

parsed_output.answer: Electric appliances are connected in parallel in a household circuit because each appliance receives the full voltage from the power supply. This ensures that each appliance operates at its rated voltage, and if one appliance fails, the others continue to function. In contrast, if appliances are connected in series, the voltage is divided among them, and if one appliance fails, the entire circuit breaks, causing all appliances to stop working. Additionally, in a series connection, the total resistance increases, which reduces the current flowing through the circuit, making it inefficient for household use.

In series, voltage is shared, total resistance rises, and all devices carry the same current

In

Then it gains kinetic energy.
This is contradictory to conservation of energy.
So our assumed clockwise

Hence the correct direction of induced
current has to be in anticlockwise direction with respect to north pole of
the bar magnet.
In such a case, the north pole of the coil faces the north pole
of the bar magnet as shown in figure 14.
Then north pole of bar magnet is
repelled by the north pole of the coil.
Hence we need to do work to overcome
this force.
This work done on the magnet is converted into electrical energy
in the coil.
In this way conservation of energy takes place in electromagnetic
induction.
Let us see a case where the bar magnet is pulled away from the coil, with
north pole facing the coil.
In such case, the coil opposes the motion of bar
magnet to balance the conversion of mechanical energy into electric energy.
This happens only when the north pole of the magnet faces the south pole of
the coil.
· Can you guess what could be the direction of induced current in the coil
in such case?
Invariably the direction of induced current in the coil must be in anti
clock wise direction.
In simple terms, when flux increases through coil, the
coil opposes the increase in the flux and when flux decreases through coil,
it opposes the decrease in the flux.
This is discovered by a Russian Physicist
Heinrich Lenz.
Lenz’s law states that “the induced current will appear in such a direction
that it opposes the changes in the flux in the coil.”

parsed_output.answer: Faraday’s law of induction explains that a changing magnetic field can induce an electromotive force (EMF) in a conductor. This can be demonstrated through an activity involving a coil, a bar magnet, and a galvanometer. When a bar magnet is moved towards or away from a coil, the galvanometer needle deflects, indicating the presence of an induced current. This happens because the relative motion between the magnet and the coil changes the magnetic flux through the coil. The induced current is in a direction that opposes the change in magnetic flux, as described by Lenz’s law. The activity shows that the induced EMF is proportional to the rate of change of magnetic flux, which is the essence of Faraday’s law of induction.

parsed_output.answer: To prove that the presence of air and water are essential for corrosion, you can perform the following experiment: Take three test tubes and place clean iron nails in each of them. Label these test tubes A, B, and C. Pour some water in test tube A and cork it. Pour boiled distilled water in test tube B, add about 1 ml of oil and cork it. The oil will float on water and prevent the air from dissolving in the water. Put some anhydrous calcium chloride in test tube C and cork it. Anhydrous calcium chloride will absorb the moisture, if any, from the air. Leave these test tubes for a few days and then observe. You will observe that iron nails rust in test tube A, but they do not rust in test tubes B and C. This experiment shows that both air and water are necessary for corrosion.

parsed_output.answer: The cleansing action of soap is due to its unique molecular structure. Soap molecules have two ends: one is hydrophilic (attracted to water) and the other is hydrophobic (attracted to grease and oil). When soap is added to water, the hydrophobic ends of the soap molecules attach to the grease and dirt on the surface of the cloth. The hydrophilic ends remain in contact with the water. With agitation, the soap molecules form clusters called micelles, which surround the dirt particles. These micelles remain suspended in water and can be rinsed away, thus cleaning the cloth.

required_point_details.point: A soap molecule has a hydrophilic ionic/polar end and hydrophobic hydrocarbon tail
Tails embed in grease while heads remain in water
Agitation forms micelles around dirt
Like-charge repulsion keeps droplets suspended
The dirt-containing micelles are washed away
